title: Refresh Token Basics
description: Understand refresh tokens and how they enable seamless user experiences without compromising security.

blocks.text: Access tokens are short-lived credentials used to access protected resources. When an access token expires, the user must authenticate again to get a new one. Refresh tokens solve this problem by allowing clients to obtain new access tokens without requiring the user to re-enter their credentials.

A refresh token is a long-lived, opaque string that the client stores securely. When the access token expires, the client sends the refresh token to an authorization server endpoint. If the refresh token is valid and has not been revoked, the server issues a new access token (and optionally a new refresh token).

blocks.title: Key Distinction
blocks.text: Access tokens are meant to be short-lived and used frequently. Refresh tokens are long-lived but used infrequently, and their sole purpose is to obtain new access tokens.

blocks.title: Benefits of Refresh Tokens
items: Improved user experience: users stay logged in without repeated authentication
Reduced credential exposure: refresh tokens are rarely transmitted compared to passwords
Fine-grained access control: servers can revoke refresh tokens at any time
Scalable token management: long-lived sessions without storing session state in memory

blocks.text: The standard refresh token flow follows these steps: (1) User authenticates with credentials. (2) Server returns an access token and a refresh token. (3) Client stores both tokens securely. (4) Client uses the access token for API requests. (5) When the access token expires, the client sends the refresh token to the token endpoint. (6) Server validates the refresh token and issues a new access token. (7) Steps 4-6 repeat until the refresh token expires or is revoked.

data.caption: Standard refresh token flow
data.definition:
sequenceDiagram
  participant User
  participant Client
  participant AuthServer
  participant ResourceServer
  User->>Client: Enters credentials
  Client->>AuthServer: POST /token (grant_type=password)
  AuthServer-->>Client: access_token + refresh_token
  Client->>ResourceServer: GET /api (Authorization: Bearer access_token)
  ResourceServer-->>Client: 200 OK
  Note over Client,AuthServer: Access token expires
  Client->>AuthServer: POST /token (grant_type=refresh_token)
  AuthServer-->>Client: new access_token
  Client->>ResourceServer: GET /api (Authorization: Bearer new access_token)
  ResourceServer-->>Client: 200 OK

blocks.text: Choosing appropriate lifetimes is critical. Access tokens typically last 5-15 minutes. Refresh tokens can last hours, days, or weeks depending on the security requirements. Short refresh token lifetimes reduce the window for abuse but require more frequent re-authentication. Long refresh token lifetimes improve user experience but increase risk if the token is stolen.

blocks.title: Security Trade-off
blocks.text: Never set refresh token lifetimes to be extremely long (months or years) without additional protections like token rotation. A stolen long-lived refresh token gives an attacker persistent access.

blocks.text: Refresh tokens can be either JWTs or opaque random strings. Opaque tokens stored server-side allow immediate revocation and are the safest choice for refresh tokens. JWT refresh tokens are stateless but require additional mechanisms like token versioning or blocklists for revocation. For high-security applications, prefer opaque refresh tokens.

blocks.title: Best Practice
blocks.text: Store refresh tokens in HTTP-only, Secure, SameSite cookies when running in a browser. This prevents JavaScript access and mitigates XSS attacks.

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
points: Refresh tokens allow clients to obtain new access tokens without user re-authentication
Access tokens should be short-lived (5-15 minutes)
Refresh tokens are long-lived but used infrequently
Prefer opaque server-side refresh tokens for revocation capability
Store refresh tokens in HTTP-only cookies in browser environments
blocks.takeaway: Refresh tokens are the backbone of seamless yet secure authentication. Understanding their role, risks, and proper implementation is essential for production applications.
